name: Tranexamic acid + niacinamide

card.summary: A combination serum pairing two brightening ingredients to fade dark spots and melasma and even out skin tone.
card.note: Oral tranexamic acid is prescription-only; topical products vary by market.

quick.overview:
Tranexamic acid and niacinamide are combined in topical serums to fade pigmentation such as melasma and post-acne marks, giving a more even skin tone. Niacinamide (vitamin B3) is a widely used cosmetic ingredient that is described as improving skin barrier function and reducing hyperpigmentation and redness, while tranexamic acid is an antifibrinolytic drug also used in dermatology for melasma.

A 2025 randomised, double-blind trial compared niosomal and conventional tranexamic acid/niacinamide creams with hydroquinone cream in melasma. A 2022 systematic review reported that combination therapies gave the best results for melasma compared with single treatments.
quick.how: The combination is used as a leave-on serum or cream, often within a routine that includes sunscreen, since melasma is sun-sensitive. Results in studies are assessed over weeks to months.
quick.risks: Topical use is generally described as well tolerated; reported effects with niacinamide include irritation. Oral tranexamic acid carries rare reported risks including blood clots and seizures and is prescription-only in many countries.

lead: Tranexamic acid plus niacinamide is a pairing of two brightening ingredients used in serums and creams to even out skin tone and fade dark patches such as melasma and post-acne marks. The idea is that the two work on different parts of the problem: tranexamic acid on pigment production, and niacinamide on the skin barrier, redness and pigment transfer, so the combination gives a clearer, more uniform complexion over weeks to months.[1][3][5]

Tranexamic acid was first synthesised in 1962 by the Japanese researchers Shosuke and Utako Okamoto. It is a synthetic lysine analogue and an antifibrinolytic that is on the WHO Model List of Essential Medicines, and it is used in medicine to reduce bleeding after trauma, in heavy periods, in childbirth and in surgery.[4] Japan permits it as a quasi-drug for skin whitening, and it is now used topically, orally and by injection in dermatology for pigmentation.[4][7] Niacinamide (nicotinamide, vitamin B3) is a long-established cosmetic ingredient described as anti-inflammatory and as improving the barrier and reducing hyperpigmentation and redness in ageing skin.[5]

Research on the pairing specifically is recent. A 2025 randomised, double-blind trial compared niosomal and conventional tranexamic acid/niacinamide creams with hydroquinone cream in melasma,[2] and a 2024 split-face randomised trial compared 3% tranexamic acid cream with 4% hydroquinone in mixed-type melasma in skin of colour.[6] A 2022 systematic review of melasma treatments found that double and triple combination therapies gave the best results compared with single treatments.[1]

On looksmaxxing forums the two ingredients mostly come up separately, with niacinamide discussed as a cheap, low-risk serum for oiliness and tone and tranexamic acid as a newer brightening option. Posters often compare them with stronger routines built around retinoids, azelaic acid and sunscreen.[8][9]

chain: Tranexamic acid and niacinamide applied together
Reduced pigment production and calmer barrier
More even tone and fading dark patches
angle.text: The pair is used to lighten melasma and dark spots and even out skin colour. Niacinamide additionally supports the barrier and reduces redness.

paras: The combination is aimed at hyperpigmentation: melasma, post-inflammatory dark marks after acne, and general unevenness of tone. Melasma is a common, chronic pigmentary disorder that appears as tan, brown or grey-brown patches, usually on the face. It is more frequent in women and in people with darker skin types, and is associated with UV exposure, hormones such as pregnancy or oral contraceptives, thyroid disease and genetics.[10] A systematic review reports prevalence of 8.8% to 40% depending on population, high recurrence, and that no single treatment is universally efficacious.[1]

Dermatology sources describe sunscreen as the base of any pigmentation routine, because ultraviolet and visible light can stimulate pigment production and small amounts of sun can bring melasma back after it has faded.[10] Topical products containing the pair are therefore usually described as one step within a routine that includes daily sun protection rather than a stand-alone fix.[10]

People use the pair for a more even complexion, fading of dark patches on the cheeks, forehead and upper lip, and a calmer, less red look. Niacinamide on its own is also used for the look of oily skin and enlarged-looking pores; a 2006 study found that 2% topical niacinamide reduced sebum excretion after two and four weeks, and a 2005 study reported improved appearance of ageing skin through less hyperpigmentation and redness.[5]

Tranexamic acid reversibly binds lysine-binding sites on plasminogen, reducing its conversion to plasmin; this antifibrinolytic action underlies its use against bleeding.[4] In skin, oral tranexamic acid has been reported to lighten melasma by reducing melanin production in epidermal melanocytes.[10] The molecule is zwitterionic, which limits penetration through the skin, so cosmetic formulations sometimes use penetration enhancers, microneedling or ester prodrugs such as cetyl tranexamate mesylate; niosomal delivery, as in the 2025 trial, is another approach.[2][4]

Niacinamide is a component of NAD+ and NADP+. In laboratory work on human keratinocytes it increased ceramide synthesis and improved the epidermal permeability barrier, and it reduced Cutibacterium acnes-induced activation of toll-like receptor 2 and interleukin-8 production, which is linked to its anti-inflammatory reputation.[5]

Nicotinamide was identified between 1935 and 1937 and is the preferred treatment for pellagra, the niacin-deficiency disease; unlike nicotinic acid it does not cause flushing. It is also on the WHO Essential Medicines list and sold over the counter in the United States.[5]

Tranexamic acid was first made in 1962 by the Okamotos, was approved in the US as an oral tablet for heavy menstrual bleeding in November 2009, and became a pharmacy medicine in the UK for that purpose in 2011.[4] Its cosmetic use grew from Japanese skin-whitening products; Wikipedia notes Japan allows it as a skin-whitening quasi-drug and that a Japanese company markets toothpaste containing it.[4]
Oral tranexamic acid is prescription-only in the United States and Australia, and sold over the counter in Japan; topical cosmetic products are regulated differently by market.[4]

On looksmax.org, niacinamide appears in skincare routine threads. One poster with a leftover 10% niacinamide bottle asked whether it was 'cope' next to a routine of tazarotene, moisturiser and sunscreen, and a reply said he might as well use it.[9] Another thread asked about reports of breakouts from niacinamide serums; one reply described using The Ordinary niacinamide with zinc and hyaluronic acid without breakouts.[8] A further thread discussed whether a vitamin C and niacinamide serum helps dark circles caused by thin skin.[11]

Topical niacinamide is described as having minimal side effects. High oral doses have been linked to liver problems, with at least one documented case of acute liver toxicity at very high intakes.[5] Reported effects of topical niacinamide in practice include irritation and, in forum anecdotes, breakouts.[8]

For tranexamic acid, side effects are rare and include seizures, colour-vision changes, blood clots and allergic reactions including anaphylaxis. Large studies have not shown increased venous or arterial thrombosis risk in medical use, though the question is debated. Contraindications include allergy, a history of seizures or thromboembolism, and severe kidney impairment.[4] Systematic reviews of melasma note that systemic tranexamic acid was associated with systemic side effects.[1] Melasma treatments can also cause irritation, lighter patches and contact dermatitis.[10]

A 2022 systematic review of melasma treatments found oral tranexamic acid promising but associated with systemic side effects, microneedling and peels effective, hydroquinone still the usual comparator, high recurrence across all groups, and the best results from double or triple combinations.[1]

A 2025 randomised, double-blind, case-controlled trial in melasma compared niosomal and conventional tranexamic acid/niacinamide creams with hydroquinone cream and assessed efficacy and safety.[2] A 2024 double-blind, split-face randomised trial compared 3% tranexamic acid cream with 4% hydroquinone cream for mixed-type melasma in skin of colour.[6] A 2023 review covers the use of tranexamic acid in dermatology.[7] As of 2017, Wikipedia notes that safety of tranexamic acid in melasma appeared reasonable while efficacy was uncertain owing to a lack of large randomised trials.[4]

Hydroquinone, which inhibits tyrosinase, is the usual comparator and is sold at 2% over the counter or 4% by prescription in the US; other melasma options include azelaic acid, kojic acid, tretinoin, peels and lasers, and triple combination creams outperformed dual therapy or hydroquinone alone in the literature summarised by Wikipedia.[10]

timeline.event: Shosuke and Utako Okamoto first make tranexamic acid.[4]
A study reports topical niacinamide improves ageing-skin appearance by reducing hyperpigmentation and redness.[5]
Oral tranexamic acid is FDA-approved in the US for heavy menstrual bleeding.[4]
UK moves the oral menstrual-bleeding product to pharmacy-medicine status.[4]
A systematic review of melasma treatments reports combination therapies gave the best results.[1]
Split-face randomised trial compares 3% tranexamic acid cream with 4% hydroquinone in skin of colour.[6]
Randomised trial tests niosomal and conventional tranexamic acid/niacinamide creams against hydroquinone.[2]

lore.intro: In these communities niacinamide is a staple budget serum, discussed alongside retinoids and sunscreen, while tranexamic acid is a newer brightening ingredient.[8][9]

claims.claim: Niacinamide serum is worth adding to a basic routine because it is cheap and helps skin look clearer.
claims.believers: Posters say it is inexpensive and use it for tone and oil, with one saying they will keep using it because it is cheap.[8][9]
claims.experts: Studies summarised on Wikipedia report reduced sebum excretion with 2% topical niacinamide and improved appearance of ageing skin with less hyperpigmentation and redness.[5]

claims.believers: A looksmax.org thread opened on reviews saying breakouts are not rare; another poster reported none.[8]
claims.experts: Reference sources describe niacinamide side effects as minimal; individual irritation is reported.[5]

claims.claim: Tranexamic acid and niacinamide together fade melasma and dark spots.
claims.believers: Skincare products sold as brightening serums pair the two ingredients on the premise that they act on different parts of pigmentation.[5]
claims.experts: A 2025 randomised trial compared such creams with hydroquinone, and a systematic review found combination therapies did best in melasma; recurrence stays high across treatments.[1][2]

claims.claim: Vitamin C plus niacinamide serum can fix dark circles caused by thin skin.
claims.believers: A looksmax.org thread title states that such a serum does not help dark circles from thin skin.[11]
claims.experts: No published study found has tested this combination for thin-skin under-eye discolouration.

claims.claim: Oral tranexamic acid is a safe route to skin lightening.
claims.believers: Oral use is discussed as a route to rapid, sustained lightening of melasma.[10]
claims.experts: Reviews call oral tranexamic acid promising for melasma but note systemic side effects; it is prescription-only in the US, and rare seizures, vision changes and clots are documented.[1][4]
